entries.1:1: This is the title line of the book, calling it the greatest of songs and linking it to Solomon. It tells the reader they are about to read a poem about love that was highly valued.
entries.1:2: The woman longs for her lover's kisses and says his love is better to her than the finest wine. It shows how deeply she desires him and how much she treasures his affection.
entries.1:3: His cologne smells wonderful, and even his name is like a sweet fragrance that draws young women to love him. It means his whole reputation is attractive and pleasant.
entries.1:4: She asks him to take her with him, and she rejoices that the king has brought her into his home. She and others celebrate his love more than wine, showing how glad she is to be chosen by him.
entries.1:5: She describes herself as dark-skinned but beautiful, comparing herself to the dark tents of Kedar and the curtains of Solomon. She is saying her looks are striking and lovely even if different from others.
entries.1:6: She explains her dark skin comes from working outside in the sun, and that her brothers were angry with her and made her tend the vineyards. It means she has had a hard life and has not even cared for her own needs.
entries.1:7: She asks her beloved where he pastures his flock and rests at midday, so she won't have to wander looking for him among other shepherds. It shows her desire to find him and not be lost among strangers.
entries.1:8: He answers her by telling her to follow the tracks of the flock and graze her young goats near the shepherds' tents. It is practical guidance that also gently teases her to go where she can find him.
entries.1:9: He compares her to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots, a picture of beauty and strength that would stand out. It means he finds her striking and exceptional.
entries.1:10: He admires her face framed by her hair and her neck adorned with jewelry. It is a compliment on her beauty and how lovely she looks decorated.
entries.1:11: Others offer to make her ornaments of gold and silver. It shows she is being honored and adorned because of her beauty.
entries.1:12: While the king sits at his table, her perfume gives off its fragrance. It suggests her presence and love quietly fill the room around him.
entries.1:13: She compares her beloved to a pouch of myrrh resting near her heart all night. It means he is precious to her and constantly on her mind.
entries.1:14: She compares her beloved to a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi. It means he is refreshing and delightful to her, like a beautiful plant in a lush place.
entries.1:15: He tells her she is beautiful and has eyes like a dove. It is a tender compliment praising her gentle, lovely appearance.
entries.1:16: She answers that he too is handsome and pleasant, and that their bed is green. It means she delights in him and in the fresh, life-filled place they share.
entries.1:17: She describes their house with cedar beams and fir boards. It pictures a sturdy, pleasant home, suggesting comfort and beauty in their life together.
entries.2:1: The woman describes herself as a simple, ordinary flower growing in plain places. It means she sees herself as modest and unremarkable, and it invites the reader to be honest about how they see themselves.
entries.2:2: The man says his beloved stands out among other women like a single lily surrounded by thorny weeds. It means he sees her as special and precious, and it shows how love makes a person treasured.
entries.2:3: She compares him to a fruit tree in a forest of ordinary trees, and says sitting in his shade and eating his fruit delighted her. It means he stands out to her and brings her joy, rest, and sweetness.
entries.2:4: He brings her into a place of celebration and openly shows his love for her like a banner. It means he is proud of her and wants everyone to know he loves her, which speaks of being loved openly and safely.
entries.2:5: She asks for food to strengthen her because her feelings of love are so strong they overwhelm her. It means love can be so powerful it feels like too much to handle, and it is okay to admit that.
entries.2:6: He holds her close, with one hand supporting her head and the other arm around her. It means she feels safe and cared for in his embrace, and it pictures the comfort of being held by someone who loves you.
entries.2:7: She urges the other women not to stir up or rush love before its proper time. It means real love should not be forced or hurried, and the reader is encouraged to let love grow at its own pace.
entries.2:8: She hears her lover coming, leaping over the mountains and hills toward her. It means he is eager and quick to reach her, and it shows the excitement of someone coming to the one they love.
entries.2:9: She describes him as swift and graceful, standing just outside the wall and peering in through the windows. It means he is close by and longing to see her, like someone waiting at the edge of her life.
entries.2:10: Her lover calls to her, telling her to get up and come out with him. It means he invites her to leave her place and join him, and it pictures love that calls a person out of isolation.
entries.2:11: He points out that winter is over and the rain has stopped. It means a hard, cold season has ended, and it gives the reader hope that difficult times do pass.
entries.2:12: Flowers are blooming, it is time to prune the vines, and doves are cooing in the land. It means new life is everywhere, and it invites the reader to notice signs of renewal around them.
entries.2:13: The fig tree is forming fruit and the vines are budding and fragrant, so he again urges her to come out. It means the season is ripe for love and new beginnings, and it encourages the reader not to miss the moment.
entries.2:14: He calls her his dove, hiding in rocky crevices, and asks her to come out so he can see her and hear her voice. It means he longs for closeness and thinks she is lovely, and it shows that being wanted includes being seen and heard.
entries.2:15: She asks that the little foxes be caught because they ruin the vines that are just starting to bear grapes. It means small problems can damage something young and growing, and it reminds the reader to guard tender things early.
entries.2:16: She says her beloved belongs to her and she belongs to him, and that he feeds among the flowers. It means their love is mutual and committed, and it pictures the simple joy of belonging to each other.
entries.2:17: She asks him to come back quickly, like a swift deer on the hills, until the cool evening arrives. It means she longs for him to stay near, and it expresses the ache of wanting someone close when they feel far away.
entries.3:1: She longs for the man she loves and searches for him through the night but cannot find him. It shows how painful it is to miss someone you deeply love.
entries.3:2: She gets up and searches the streets of the city for the one she loves, but still cannot find him. It pictures how far love will go to find the person it longs for.
entries.3:3: She asks the night guards if they have seen the man she loves. It shows her turning to others for help in her search.
entries.3:4: Soon after, she finds him and holds on to him, bringing him to her mother's home. It shows the joy and relief of being reunited with the one you love.
entries.3:5: She urges the other women not to stir up love before the right time. It is a reminder to let love grow and wait for the proper moment.
entries.3:6: People wonder who this is coming from the wilderness surrounded by fragrant smoke and spices. It creates a picture of someone grand and richly perfumed approaching.
entries.3:7: It is Solomon's own carriage or bed, guarded by sixty fighting men of Israel. It shows the king surrounded by protection and honor.
entries.3:8: Each guard carries a sword and is trained for battle, ready because of dangers at night. It shows how carefully the king is protected.
entries.3:9: King Solomon had a special carriage made from the wood of Lebanon. It points to his wealth and care in making something fine.
entries.3:10: The carriage is decorated with silver, gold, purple fabric, and ebony. It shows the beauty and luxury of what was made for the king.
entries.3:11: She invites the other women to look at King Solomon wearing the crown his mother gave him on his wedding day. It celebrates the joy and honor of a wedding.
entries.4:1: The man praises the woman's beauty, comparing her eyes to a dove and her hair to a flock of goats resting on a hillside. It means he sees her as lovely and tells her so plainly.
entries.4:2: He compares her teeth to freshly washed sheep, each with its twin, meaning her teeth are clean, even, and complete. It is a picture of health and beauty.
entries.4:3: Her lips and mouth are praised as striking and lovely, and her cheeks behind her veil are compared to pomegranate fruit. He is describing her face as beautiful.
entries.4:4: Her neck is compared to a strong tower hung with shields, suggesting dignity and strength. He admires her as noble and impressive.
entries.4:5: Her breasts are compared to two young deer feeding among lilies, a gentle picture of youth and beauty. He is praising her form with tender imagery.
entries.4:6: He says he will go to fragrant mountains until the evening cool comes, meaning he intends to stay near her and enjoy her sweetness. It expresses longing and delight.
entries.4:7: He tells her she is completely beautiful with no flaw in his eyes. It is a wholehearted statement of love and admiration.
entries.4:8: He invites her to come with him from the high mountains where lions and leopards live, calling her his bride. It is a call to leave danger and be with him.
entries.4:9: He says she has captured his heart with a single glance and a single ornament of her neck. It means she has completely won his love.
entries.4:10: He says her love is better than wine and the scent of her oils better than any perfume. He is saying she delights him more than anything else.
entries.4:11: He describes her lips as sweet as honey and her clothes as fragrant as Lebanon. It means everything about her is pleasant and appealing to him.
entries.4:12: He calls her a walled garden and a sealed spring, meaning she is private, precious, and kept for him alone. It speaks of her purity and his exclusive love.
entries.4:13: He describes her as a garden full of pomegranates and fine fruits with fragrant plants. It means she is rich and full of good things.
entries.4:14: He lists many costly spices growing in her garden, meaning she is full of rare and delightful qualities. He is praising her richness and worth.
entries.4:15: He calls her a fountain of gardens and a spring of fresh flowing water. It means she is a source of life and refreshment to him.
entries.4:16: She asks the winds to blow on her garden so its fragrance spreads, and invites her beloved to come and enjoy its fruits. It is her open welcome to him.
entries.5:1: The man says he has come into his garden and enjoyed its gifts, and he invites his friends to share the feast and celebrate love. It pictures love as something good to be enjoyed and shared openly.
entries.5:2: She is asleep but aware of her lover knocking at the door, calling her his sister, love, and dove, and complaining that his hair is wet with night dew. It shows a lover arriving tired and longing to be let in.
entries.5:3: She hesitates, saying she has already taken off her coat and washed her feet and does not want to get up and dirty them again. It captures the small, lazy excuse we make when someone we love asks something of us.
entries.5:4: Her lover reaches through the opening of the door, and her heart softens toward him. It shows how a small gesture from someone we love can move us deeply.
entries.5:5: She gets up to open the door, and her hands drip with myrrh as she reaches the lock. It pictures her preparing herself with care and fragrance to welcome him.
entries.5:6: When she opens the door he has already left, and she is crushed; she searches for him and calls him but gets no answer. It shows the pain of missed timing and the ache of losing someone we love.
entries.5:7: The night watchmen of the city find her, beat her, and take her veil. It shows that her search for love leaves her exposed and hurt by others.
entries.5:8: She asks the other women to tell her lover, if they find him, that she is sick with love for him. It shows her openly admitting how much she longs for him.
entries.5:9: The other women ask her what makes her lover so special compared to any other man. It sets up her chance to explain why he matters so much to her.
entries.5:10: She answers that her lover stands out among thousands, healthy and strong in appearance. It shows her seeing him as unique and precious above everyone else.
entries.5:11: She describes his head as fine gold and his hair as thick and black like a raven. It is her way of praising his handsome appearance.
entries.5:12: She compares his eyes to doves beside streams of water, clean and well placed. It is a poetic way of saying his eyes are gentle and beautiful.
entries.5:13: She likens his face to beds of spices giving off sweet smells and his lips to lilies dripping myrrh. It shows how pleasant and appealing she finds everything about him.
entries.5:14: She describes his hands as gold set with jewels and his body as smooth ivory decorated with sapphires. It is her poetic praise of his strength and beauty.
entries.5:15: She compares his legs to stone pillars on gold bases and his appearance to the majestic mountains of Lebanon and its cedars. It shows she sees him as strong, steady, and impressive.
entries.5:16: She says his mouth is sweet and he is altogether beautiful, then tells the women that this is her lover and her friend. It sums up her wholehearted love and the friendship she shares with him.
entries.6:1: The women ask the woman where her lover has gone, offering to help her find him. It shows friends caring about her search and wanting to help.
entries.6:2: She answers that he has gone to his garden to enjoy its spices and gather lilies. For the reader, it pictures love as something private and delightful, not lost.
entries.6:3: She says they belong to each other, and he is enjoying his garden among the lilies. It means mutual love and belonging, a picture of closeness and commitment.
entries.6:4: He praises her beauty by comparing her to two cities and to an army with banners. It means she is striking and impressive, so the reader sees strong admiration in love.
entries.6:5: He asks her to look away because her eyes overwhelm him, then praises her hair like goats resting on a hillside. It means her beauty is powerful to him, showing how love makes someone deeply affecting.
entries.6:6: He compares her teeth to a flock of sheep coming from washing, each with its twin. It means her teeth are clean, even, and complete, a picture of health and beauty.
entries.6:7: He compares the sides of her head under her veil to pomegranate fruit. It means her features are lovely and fresh, continuing his praise of her beauty.
entries.6:8: He mentions many queens, wives, and young women without number. It means there are many beautiful women, setting up his point that she stands out above them all.
entries.6:9: He says his dove is unique and the favorite of her mother, praised by other women. It means she is special and treasured, and the reader sees how love singles someone out.
entries.6:10: Others ask who this woman is, bright as dawn, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and impressive as an army. It means her beauty and presence are striking and admired by everyone.
entries.6:11: He went down to the nut garden to check on the valley's plants and see if vines and pomegranates were blooming. It means he was looking for signs of life and growth, a picture of hopeful watching.
entries.6:12: The verse breaks off before he was aware of it, leaving the thought unfinished. It means something happened suddenly and unexpectedly, and the reader senses surprise or a shift in the moment.
entries.6:13: Others call the woman to come back so they can see her, and someone asks what they see in her, answering with a dance. It means she is being called to be seen and admired, pictured as lively and celebrated.
entries.7:1: The man praises the woman's beauty from her feet upward, comparing her graceful form to fine craftsmanship. It means she is deeply valued and admired by the one who loves her.
entries.7:2: He uses images of grain and wine to describe her body as rich and life-giving. For the reader, it shows love that celebrates the beloved with warm, generous praise.
entries.7:3: He compares her breasts to twin young deer, a picture of symmetry and youthful beauty. It is simply part of the poem's admiring description of the woman he loves.
entries.7:4: Her neck, eyes, and nose are compared to strong towers and clear pools, mixing strength and beauty. The point is that every feature of the beloved is striking and worthy of praise.
entries.7:5: Her head and hair are pictured as majestic, and her hair holds the king captive. It means her beauty has completely won the heart of the one who loves her.
entries.7:6: He sums up his praise by calling her beautiful and delightful. It shows love that openly expresses joy and pleasure in the beloved.
entries.7:7: He compares her tall figure to a palm tree and her breasts to clusters of fruit. The image conveys growth, beauty, and promise.
entries.7:8: He longs to draw close to her, describing her as sweet as fruit and fragrant as apples. It expresses strong desire joined with tender admiration.
entries.7:9: Her mouth is compared to the smoothest wine, flowing gently for the one she loves. It pictures affection that is pleasant and refreshing to share.
entries.7:10: The woman declares that she belongs to her beloved and that he longs for her. It is a simple, confident statement of mutual love and belonging.
entries.7:11: She invites her beloved to go out together into the fields and rest among the trees. It shows love that enjoys shared time and simple places.
entries.7:12: She suggests rising early to see the vineyards and blossoms, promising her love there. It pictures love that is eager, fresh, and tied to the beauty of creation.
entries.7:13: She says sweet-smelling plants and stored fruits are ready, kept for her beloved. It means she has saved her love and delight to share with him alone.
entries.8:1: She wishes she could show her love openly like a sister would, without people disapproving. It shows how much she longs for her affection to be accepted rather than judged.
entries.8:2: She pictures bringing him home to her mother's house to be taught and to share sweet wine together. It means she wants their love to be welcomed by her family and celebrated openly.
entries.8:3: This image of his arms holding her close shows tender, protective love. It means she feels safe and cherished in his embrace.
entries.8:4: She urges the younger women not to rush into love before its proper time. It means real love is worth waiting for rather than forcing.
entries.8:5: She is seen coming from the wilderness leaning on her beloved, and she recalls where his life began. It means love involves deep closeness and remembering where each person came from.
entries.8:6: She asks to be kept close to his heart and marked on his arm, because love is as powerful as death and burns fiercely. It means true love is intense, lasting, and not something to take lightly.
entries.8:7: No amount of water can drown love, and no wealth can buy it. It means genuine love cannot be destroyed or purchased, so it should be valued above money.
entries.8:8: The family wonders what to do for their young sister who is not yet grown. It means they are thinking ahead about how to care for her when she is old enough to marry.
entries.8:9: If she stands firm like a wall they will honor her, but if she is open like a door they will protect her. It means the family will either celebrate her strength or guard her when she is vulnerable.
entries.8:10: She says she has become like a strong wall with towers, and he saw her as one who found favor. It means she has grown into maturity and feels valued by the one she loves.
entries.8:11: Solomon owned a vineyard and rented it out, with each tenant paying a large amount of silver for its fruit. It sets up a comparison about who truly owns and enjoys what is valuable.
entries.8:12: She says her own vineyard is hers to keep, while Solomon can have his payment and the workers their share. It means she values what is truly her own and is content with her place.
entries.8:13: She asks her beloved, who rests among the gardens, to let her hear his voice while friends listen. It means she longs for his words and for closeness with him.
entries.8:14: She invites her loved one to come quickly, like a swift deer on the spice-filled mountains. It means she eagerly longs for him to come to her.
